architectural_implications.after: A single instrumentation hook that emits structured spans for every agent step, feeding both a trace UI and downstream eval jobs.
architectural_implications.before: Ad-hoc console logging and hand-written log lines interleaved with agent logic.
architectural_implications.consequence: Span schema becomes a shared contract; changing it breaks eval pipelines and golden dataset linkage, so the trace format needs versioning discipline.
architectural_implications.observation: Trace collection is decoupled from agent code via OpenInference/OpenTelemetry module registration.

architectural_implications.after: A curated, versioned set of 20-100 human-labeled traces that judges are validated against and experiments are run over.
architectural_implications.before: Eval inputs approximated by whatever prompts the developer had on hand.
architectural_implications.consequence: Labeling throughput and dataset curation become roadmap-critical; the dataset must be refreshed as usage patterns drift, or the eval suite grades yesterday's failures.
architectural_implications.observation: The golden dataset becomes a first-class artifact, produced by annotating traces in the observability platform.

architectural_implications.after: Two-tier pipeline: judge produces labels, a labeled golden set measures the judge's precision/recall, and only a validated judge feeds CI.
architectural_implications.before: One evaluation pass — the LLM judge's verdict is taken as the quality signal.
architectural_implications.consequence: Adds a calibration loop and per-judge maintenance burden, but makes failures in the grader auditable instead of invisible.
architectural_implications.observation: A meta-eval layer exists above the agent: the judge is itself tested against human labels before its scores gate the build.

architectural_implications.after: Experiments against a golden dataset run in GitHub Actions, and the build fails on acceptance-criteria metrics.
architectural_implications.before: Ship after a few manual runs; quality regressions discovered in production by users.
architectural_implications.consequence: CI runtime and API spend rise, and non-determinism must be handled with repeated runs and pass@k / pass^k-style metrics rather than a single sample.
architectural_implications.observation: Prompt/agent changes move behind a statistical acceptance gate in CI/CD rather than manual sign-off.

article_ideas.angle: Treat the judge as the system under test: per-class agreement, degenerate-predictor detection, and the XML-delimiter flip as a case study in silent total failure.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers and platform teams building automated quality gates for LLM agents
article_ideas.based_on: metric stability is not evidence of correctness
article_ideas.thesis: An LLM judge is an untested classifier until it has been scored against a human-labeled golden set; because a systematically wrong judge produces stable, low-variance scores, metric consistency is actively misleading evidence of correctness and calibration must precede gating.
article_ideas.title: Your Judge Is a Model, Not an Oracle

article_ideas.angle: Build the eval suite as a test pyramid with an explicit routing rule per assertion, and show where exact matching silently misgrades semantic quality.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leads owning eval-suite cost and CI runtime
article_ideas.based_on: Routing each assertion to the cheapest sufficient mechanism
article_ideas.thesis: Most eval suites route assertions to the wrong mechanism; partitioning by decidability — deterministic checks first, judges only on outputs that survive — cuts suite cost and runtime by orders of magnitude while increasing semantic coverage where it actually matters.
article_ideas.title: Stop Paying an LLM to Check Your JSON

article_ideas.angle: Frame CI gating as a statistical policy decision — repeated runs, pass@k versus pass^k, threshold selection — and treat golden-dataset refresh as roadmap-critical maintenance.
article_ideas.audience: Teams moving agent development from manual spot-checks to CI/CD
article_ideas.based_on: Eval prompts are treated as production code
article_ideas.thesis: Once eval prompts are versioned like code and acceptance metrics gate CI, the hardest remaining problem is statistical rather than editorial: non-deterministic scores plus a small golden set make every threshold a choice between flaky builds and undetected regressions.
article_ideas.title: The Prompt Diff Is the Release Gate

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the design question from 'how do we write a good eval' to 'what does each layer catch that the others don't', and justify paying for redundant coverage.
article_ideas.audience: Staff engineers and architects designing agent quality systems
article_ideas.thesis: For open-ended agent failure surfaces, coverage comes from heterogeneous detectors with uncorrelated blind spots — automated evals, human review, production monitoring — not from optimizing a single eval to exhaustion.
article_ideas.title: Depth in Layers, Not Accuracy in One Metric

connections.concept: LLM-as-a-judge validation against a golden dataset
connections.connects_to: classifier evaluation practice (precision/recall on labeled data)
connections.relationship: Judges are classifiers with a semantic label space, so standard supervised-evaluation discipline transfers directly — including the need for per-class agreement and awareness of degenerate constant predictors.

connections.concept: Code evals + LLM judges + human labels
connections.relationship: Mirrors the classic test pyramid: cheap deterministic checks gate fast, expensive semantic checks run on survivors, humans resolve ground truth and sample the rest.
Turns observability data into an agent input, making the observability schema a prompt-adjacent interface that must be complete and well-structured.
Borrowed from safety engineering: reliability comes from uncorrelated failure modes across layers rather than from maximizing any single layer's accuracy.
Gating requires aggregating multiple sampled runs, so release policy becomes a statistical threshold problem rather than a boolean assertion.

evidence_quotes.text: Adding XML tags around few-shot examples flipped the evaluator's classification results from all negative to correct.
Build a golden dataset of 20-100 human-labeled examples to test your judges.
Validate LLM judges against human-labeled golden datasets.

core_insights.generalization: Any LLM used as a grader, router, or classifier in an automated pipeline needs its own labeled test set and per-class agreement metrics; delimiter/formatting sensitivity is a first-class regression surface, and metric stability is not evidence of correctness.
core_insights.insight: An LLM judge is itself an untested model: it must be validated against a human-labeled golden set before its scores are trusted, and its failure mode can be silent and degenerate. In the workshop, adding XML delimiters around few-shot examples flipped an evaluator's classifications from uniformly negative to correct — meaning the judge had been systematically wrong, not merely noisy.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Judges sit in the trust path of every automated quality metric and CI gate. A judge that emits a constant label (all pass or all fail) looks stable and low-variance, so it evades detection by the usual 'the numbers look consistent' heuristic, while silently invalidating every downstream decision. This makes judge calibration a prerequisite, not an optimization.

evidence_quotes.text: Reading traces doesn't scale, but your coding agent does.

core_insights.generalization: As agent systems generate more telemetry than humans can review, the analysis layer itself becomes an agentic workload; observability infrastructure should be optimized for machine consumers (structured spans, stable schemas) as much as for human dashboards.
core_insights.insight: The human bottleneck in observability is not collecting traces but reading them, and the proposed substitute is a coding agent reading traces on your behalf rather than a human skimming transcripts.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This reframes 'manual trace review' from a human ritual into an automated analysis stage that can operate over hundreds of spans, keeping qualitative inspection in the loop without it becoming the scaling limit. It also implies the trace format must be machine-readable and complete enough for an agent to reason over — a constraint on instrumentation design, not just tooling choice.

evidence_quotes.text: Code evals run in milliseconds and cost nothing.
Code evals are fast, free, and brittle (deterministic checks).
LLM judge evals understand meaning, use rubrics, cost money, and are non-deterministic.
Humans are the gold standard for quality but do not scale.

core_insights.generalization: In any verification system, partition assertions by whether they are decidable and cheap versus semantic and expensive; layer the cheap layer first so the expensive layer only runs on outputs that already pass structural checks.
core_insights.insight: Eval type should be selected by the property being tested, not by preference: deterministic code checks own format/structure/required content in milliseconds at zero cost, LLM judges own semantics (correctness, faithfulness, tone, actionability) at a cost in money and determinism, and humans own ground truth at a cost in scale.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Teams routinely pay LLM-judge latency and cost for checks that a string match would settle (e.g., 'does the output mention the requested ticker'), or conversely rely on brittle exact matching for semantic qualities. Routing each assertion to the cheapest sufficient mechanism changes eval suite cost and runtime by orders of magnitude.

evidence_quotes.text: Treat eval prompts like code.
Gate your CI/CD build on acceptance criteria metrics.
Without evals, every prompt change is a gamble.

core_insights.generalization: Any system with non-deterministic outputs needs a statistical acceptance gate in CI rather than a deterministic test suite; the gate's threshold policy becomes an architectural decision, not a tooling detail.
core_insights.insight: Eval prompts are treated as production code and their acceptance metrics become build gates: experiments run against a golden dataset, and CI/CD fails when scores fall below acceptance criteria rather than when a human feels the diff is fine.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This converts prompt/model/agent changes from an unreviewable diff into a measurable regression surface with a pass/fail boundary. It also introduces a new maintenance burden — the eval suite and golden dataset must be versioned alongside the agent — and forces a decision about how to threshold non-deterministic scores.

core_insights.generalization: Observability for agent runtimes should be a middleware/instrumentation layer conforming to a shared semantic convention, so that traces are a stable substrate consumable by debuggers, eval harnesses, and dataset builders alike.
core_insights.insight: Tracing is treated as an auto-instrumentation concern (~5 lines registering an SDK module) emitting OpenInference/OpenTelemetry spans, rather than manual logging statements scattered through agent code.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Putting trace emission at the SDK/module boundary keeps observability out of business logic and produces uniform span structure across agent steps, which is what makes traces reusable as eval inputs and dataset material. Manual logging couples instrumentation to code churn and yields inconsistent schemas.

evidence_quotes.text: Stacking multiple imperfect evaluation layers so that errors are caught by at least one layer.
Automated evals
Manual transcript review
Production monitoring and A/B testing

core_insights.generalization: For systems with open-ended failure surfaces, coverage comes from heterogeneous detectors with uncorrelated blind spots, not from maximizing the accuracy of a single detector.
core_insights.insight: Quality is engineered as stacked imperfect layers — automated evals, manual transcript review, production monitoring and A/B testing — on the assumption that each layer misses different failures, so no single eval is expected to be sufficient.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This shifts the design question from 'how do we write a good eval' to 'what does each layer catch that the others don't,' which justifies paying for redundant coverage (e.g., an LLM judge plus sampled human review plus live monitoring) instead of optimizing one metric to exhaustion.

A judge that always emits the same label looks low-variance and therefore 'stable', so the usual consistency heuristic cannot catch it; only a human-labeled golden set with per-class agreement can. Without this, CI gates certify nothing.

If a formatting change can flip an evaluator from uniformly wrong to correct, the reverse can happen in production with no signal. This makes judge prompts a versioned artifact needing perturbation tests, not a one-time authoring task.

open_questions.why_unresolved: The workshop demonstrates a 16-trace annotation and recommends 20-100 labeled examples, but the summary gives no agreement statistics or confidence intervals tying label count to gate reliability.

open_questions.question: How brittle are judges to prompt formatting beyond delimiter placement, and how would drift be detected in production?
open_questions.research_direction: Perturbation testing of judge prompts (delimiters, ordering, whitespace, few-shot count) scored against the golden set, plus periodic re-validation jobs to detect degradation after model updates.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The XML-tag flip is a single anecdote; no systematic sensitivity testing or monitoring for judge drift is described.

project_ideas.based_on: Build a golden dataset of 20-100 human-labeled examples to test your judges.
project_ideas.hypothesis: For a given judge and task, precision/recall estimated from a human-labeled golden set of N examples converges tightly enough at a specific N to support a build gate, and a constant-label judge will be detected by per-class agreement even though its run-to-run variance is near zero.
project_ideas.measurement: Confidence-interval width on precision/recall versus golden-set size; detection rate of the constant-label control judge; false-certification rate at each set size.
project_ideas.name: Judge Certifier
project_ideas.poc: Take 100 traces from a real agent, hand-label them, then sweep golden-set size (10, 20, 40, 80) and measure variance in judge precision/recall estimates. Include a deliberately degenerate judge that always returns 'pass' as a control to confirm the variance-based heuristic misses it while per-class agreement flags it.

project_ideas.based_on: Adding XML tags around few-shot examples flipped the evaluator's classification results from all negative to correct.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Non-semantic perturbations to a judge prompt (delimiter style, few-shot ordering, few-shot count, whitespace) cause classification flips on a labeled golden set at a measurable rate, and that flip rate varies more across perturbations than across repeated runs of a single prompt.
project_ideas.measurement: Per-perturbation accuracy delta and flip rate versus human labels; ratio of perturbation-induced variance to sampling variance across repeated identical runs.
project_ideas.name: Judge Perturbation Fuzzer
project_ideas.poc: Generate a matrix of judge-prompt variants around one task, run each against a fixed labeled set, and score agreement with human labels. Report per-perturbation deltas to rank which formatting dimensions are the real regression surface.

project_ideas.based_on: Gate your CI/CD build on acceptance criteria metrics.
project_ideas.hypothesis: For the same agent and golden set, pass^k with a moderate threshold strictly dominates single-run scoring on regression escape rate per CI dollar, and the dominant cost driver is repeated sampling rather than judge pricing.
project_ideas.measurement: False-alarm rate, regression escape rate, CI wall-clock time, and API spend per gate configuration per injected regression.
project_ideas.name: Gate Policy Bench
project_ideas.poc: Inject a known set of quality regressions into an agent, then run three gate configurations — single-run threshold, pass@k, pass^k — in CI against the same golden dataset and record which regressions each gate catches and which good builds it blocks.

project_ideas.based_on: Reading traces doesn't scale, but your coding agent does.
project_ideas.hypothesis: A coding agent reading structured OpenInference spans agrees with human reviewers on labeled traces at a rate high enough to substitute for manual transcript reading, but exhibits a measurable rate of confidently wrong diagnoses that must be reported rather than hidden.
project_ideas.measurement: Detection rate on known-bad traces, false-positive rate on good traces, confident-but-wrong diagnosis rate, and cost per trace compared to human review time.
project_ideas.name: Agent Trace Triage
project_ideas.poc: Assemble a labeled trace set containing known-bad and known-good agent runs, have both a human reviewer and an agent-driven triage harness diagnose each trace, and compare diagnoses against the ground-truth labels.

source.author: AI Engineer
source.title: How to Know If Your AI Agent Is Any Good: Evals With Phoenix & Claude — Laurie Voss, Arize AI

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Laurie Voss
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Evaluating LLM agents using Phoenix and Claude
  • Purpose: To guide AI engineers on moving past 'vibes-based' agent development to systematic, automated evaluation using Phoenix and CI/CD pipelines. Laurie Voss, Head of Developer Relations at Arize AI, presents a comprehensive workshop on how to evaluate AI agents using Phoenix and the Claude Agent SDK in TypeScript. He introduces a 7-step process starting from tracing agent steps, reading and organizing data, writing code and LLM-as-a-judge evals, testing the judge against human labels, running experiments, and locking them into CI/CD pipelines.

Topic Map

Introduction & Setup

  • Explanation: Introduction of speaker Laurie Voss, setting up the workshop repo using TypeScript, Node 22, and Phoenix on localhost:6006.
  • Key claims:
    • AI agents need traces and evals to know if changes make them better or worse.
    • Without evals, every prompt change is a gamble.
  • Examples:
    • GitHub repo seldo/aie-nyc
  • Terminology:
    • Traces
    • Evals
    • Phoenix
    • OpenInference
    • OpenTelemetry
  • Why it matters: Establish foundational tooling for tracking and evaluating AI agent behavior.

What Are Evals?

  • Explanation: Defining traces as logs for AI and evals as tests for AI, contrasting them with unit tests.
  • Key claims:
    • Traces record what your AI did at an incredible level of detail.
    • Evals run tests on your traces to see if the output is any good.
    • LLMs are non-deterministic, so traditional unit tests don't work.
  • Examples:
    • Comparing LLM output stability across multiple runs
  • Terminology:
    • Traces
    • Evals
    • Spans
    • Non-deterministic
  • Why it matters: Provides the core mental model for AI observability and testing.

Types of Evals: Code, LLM Judge, and Human

  • Explanation: Breaking down the three types of evaluations: code evals, LLM-as-a-judge evals, and human evaluations.
  • Key claims:
    • Code evals are fast, free, and brittle (deterministic checks).
    • LLM judge evals understand meaning, use rubrics, cost money, and are non-deterministic.
    • Humans are the gold standard for quality but do not scale.
  • Examples:
    • Checking JSON parsing with code eval
    • Checking tone and grounding with LLM judge
  • Terminology:
    • Code evals
    • LLM-as-a-judge
    • Rubric
    • Gold standard
  • Why it matters: Shows how to combine complementary evaluation approaches for robustness.

Step 1 & 2: Tracing and Reading Data

  • Explanation: Instrumenting the Claude Agent SDK with Phoenix using OpenInference and OpenTelemetry, and reading traces.
  • Key claims:
    • Tracing takes about 5 lines of code using OpenInference.
    • Reading traces doesn't scale, but your coding agent does.
  • Examples:
    • Registering ClaudeAgentSDKModule with Phoenix
  • Terminology:
    • OpenTelemetry
    • OpenInference
    • Spans
    • Manual instrumentation
  • Why it matters: Enables automatic collection of agent behavior without manual logging.

Step 3: Code Evals

  • Explanation: Writing deterministic TypeScript code evals for structural and format requirements.
  • Key claims:
    • Code evals run in milliseconds and cost nothing.
    • They check formatting, structure, and required content.
  • Examples:
    • Checking if output mentions the requested stock ticker
  • Terminology:
    • Code evals
    • Determinism
  • Why it matters: Provides fast, inexpensive checks for basic output structure.

Step 4 & 5: LLM-as-a-Judge and Writing Your Own Judge

  • Explanation: Using Phoenix built-in evaluations and writing custom LLM judges using rubrics and few-shot examples.
  • Key claims:
    • LLM judges evaluate semantic qualities like correctness, faithfulness, and actionability.
    • A good eval prompt needs the judge's role, explicit criteria, marked data, labeled examples, and a constrained answer.
  • Examples:
    • Creating an actionability evaluator with binary choices
  • Terminology:
    • LLM-as-a-judge
    • Rubric
    • Precision
    • Recall
    • Golden dataset
  • Why it matters: Automates semantic evaluation of agent performance at scale.

Step 6, 7 & 8: Testing Evals, Experiments, and CI/CD

  • Explanation: Running experiments against golden datasets and integrating test suites into GitHub Actions CI.
  • Key claims:
    • Treat eval prompts like code.
    • Gate your CI/CD build on acceptance criteria metrics.
  • Examples:
    • Running npm test and npm run experiment in GitHub Actions
  • Terminology:
    • Golden dataset
    • Experiments
    • CI/CD
    • Pass@k
    • Pass^k
  • Why it matters: Prevents regressions when modifying prompts, models, or agent code in production.

Key Points

Looks good to me is not a test suite

  • Explanation: Relying on manual spot-checking of a few agent runs leads to unexpected production failures when users use the agent in novel ways.
  • Evidence: Shipping agent features based on 3 manual test runs.
  • Practical implication: Establish automated evaluation suites before shipping AI agents.

Code evals are fast, free, and brittle

  • Explanation: Deterministic functions check formatting and exact matches in milliseconds without API costs.
  • Evidence: String matching and JSON parsing checks.
  • Practical implication: Use code evals for structure and format; use LLM judges for meaning.

LLM judges understand meaning but make mistakes

  • Explanation: Using a second LLM to grade outputs against a rubric handles semantics but can be non-deterministic and costly.
  • Evidence: LLM judge evaluating grounding and tone.
  • Practical implication: Validate LLM judges against human-labeled golden datasets.

Human labels form the golden dataset

  • Explanation: Humans remain the gold standard for quality judgment.
  • Evidence: Annotating 16 traces with actionability labels in Phoenix.
  • Practical implication: Build a golden dataset of 20-100 human-labeled examples to test your judges.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Swiss Cheese Model of Quality

  • How it works: Stacking multiple imperfect evaluation layers so that errors are caught by at least one layer.
  • Components:
    • Automated evals
    • Manual transcript review
    • Production monitoring and A/B testing
  • When to use: When building production-grade AI agents requiring high reliability.

Five Parts of a Good Eval Prompt

  • How it works: Structuring an LLM judge prompt for consistent, reliable grading.
  • Components:
    • The judge's role
    • Explicit criteria
    • Data clearly marked
    • Labeled examples
    • A constrained answer
  • When to use: When writing custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators.

Examples & Case Studies

An agent searching for Tesla data returned a report about an 18th-century inventor instead.

  • Illustrates: Confidently wrong model behavior.
  • Lesson: Without evals, model hallucinations and confabulations go unnoticed until customers experience them.

Adding XML tags around few-shot examples flipped the evaluator's classification results from all negative to correct.

  • Illustrates: Prompt sensitivity in LLM judges.
  • Lesson: Treat eval prompts like code; structure data clearly using XML tags to avoid parsing confusion.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Read your traces before writing evals.
    • Write code evals for structure and format.
    • Add LLM-as-a-judge evals for semantic quality.
  • Strategic:
    • Build a golden dataset with human-labeled examples.
    • Run experiments when changing prompts or models.
    • Integrate test suites into CI/CD pipelines.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How many examples are needed in the golden dataset?
    • How to balance precision and recall in LLM judges?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Tracing takes about five lines of code using OpenInference. (technical)
  • Human-human agreement on qualitative tasks (Cohen's kappa) is often low (0.2-0.3). (statistical)

Notable Quotes

"Without evals, every change is a gamble." (at 11:49) ""Looks good to me" is not a test suite." (at 10:12) "A prompt change you haven't measured is a vibe." (at 165:10)

Compressed Summary

  • Traces are logs; evals are tests for AI.

summary.markdown:
## Overview
- **Speaker**: Laurie Voss
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Evaluating LLM agents using Phoenix and Claude
- **Purpose**: To guide AI engineers on moving past 'vibes-based' agent development to systematic, automated evaluation using Phoenix and CI/CD pipelines.
Laurie Voss, Head of Developer Relations at Arize AI, presents a comprehensive workshop on how to evaluate AI agents using Phoenix and the Claude Agent SDK in TypeScript. He introduces a 7-step process starting from tracing agent steps, reading and organizing data, writing code and LLM-as-a-judge evals, testing the judge against human labels, running experiments, and locking them into CI/CD pipelines.
## Topic Map
### Introduction & Setup
- **Explanation**: Introduction of speaker Laurie Voss, setting up the workshop repo using TypeScript, Node 22, and Phoenix on localhost:6006.
- **Key claims**:
  - AI agents need traces and evals to know if changes make them better or worse.
  - Without evals, every prompt change is a gamble.
- **Examples**:
  - GitHub repo seldo/aie-nyc
- **Terminology**:
  - Traces
  - Evals
  - Phoenix
  - OpenInference
  - OpenTelemetry
- **Why it matters**: Establish foundational tooling for tracking and evaluating AI agent behavior.
### What Are Evals?
- **Explanation**: Defining traces as logs for AI and evals as tests for AI, contrasting them with unit tests.
- **Key claims**:
  - Traces record what your AI did at an incredible level of detail.
  - Evals run tests on your traces to see if the output is any good.
  - LLMs are non-deterministic, so traditional unit tests don't work.
- **Examples**:
  - Comparing LLM output stability across multiple runs
- **Terminology**:
  - Traces
  - Evals
  - Spans
  - Non-deterministic
- **Why it matters**: Provides the core mental model for AI observability and testing.
### Types of Evals: Code, LLM Judge, and Human
- **Explanation**: Breaking down the three types of evaluations: code evals, LLM-as-a-judge evals, and human evaluations.
- **Key claims**:
  - Code evals are fast, free, and brittle (deterministic checks).
  - LLM judge evals understand meaning, use rubrics, cost money, and are non-deterministic.
  - Humans are the gold standard for quality but do not scale.
- **Examples**:
  - Checking JSON parsing with code eval
  - Checking tone and grounding with LLM judge
- **Terminology**:
  - Code evals
  - LLM-as-a-judge
  - Rubric
  - Gold standard
- **Why it matters**: Shows how to combine complementary evaluation approaches for robustness.
### Step 1 & 2: Tracing and Reading Data
- **Explanation**: Instrumenting the Claude Agent SDK with Phoenix using OpenInference and OpenTelemetry, and reading traces.
- **Key claims**:
  - Tracing takes about 5 lines of code using OpenInference.
  - Reading traces doesn't scale, but your coding agent does.
- **Examples**:
  - Registering ClaudeAgentSDKModule with Phoenix
- **Terminology**:
  - OpenTelemetry
  - OpenInference
  - Spans
  - Manual instrumentation
- **Why it matters**: Enables automatic collection of agent behavior without manual logging.
### Step 3: Code Evals
- **Explanation**: Writing deterministic TypeScript code evals for structural and format requirements.
- **Key claims**:
  - Code evals run in milliseconds and cost nothing.
  - They check formatting, structure, and required content.
- **Examples**:
  - Checking if output mentions the requested stock ticker
- **Terminology**:
  - Code evals
  - Determinism
- **Why it matters**: Provides fast, inexpensive checks for basic output structure.
### Step 4 & 5: LLM-as-a-Judge and Writing Your Own Judge
- **Explanation**: Using Phoenix built-in evaluations and writing custom LLM judges using rubrics and few-shot examples.
- **Key claims**:
  - LLM judges evaluate semantic qualities like correctness, faithfulness, and actionability.
  - A good eval prompt needs the judge's role, explicit criteria, marked data, labeled examples, and a constrained answer.
- **Examples**:
  - Creating an actionability evaluator with binary choices
- **Terminology**:
  - LLM-as-a-judge
  - Rubric
  - Precision
  - Recall
  - Golden dataset
- **Why it matters**: Automates semantic evaluation of agent performance at scale.
### Step 6, 7 & 8: Testing Evals, Experiments, and CI/CD
- **Explanation**: Running experiments against golden datasets and integrating test suites into GitHub Actions CI.
- **Key claims**:
  - Treat eval prompts like code.
  - Gate your CI/CD build on acceptance criteria metrics.
- **Examples**:
  - Running npm test and npm run experiment in GitHub Actions
- **Terminology**:
  - Golden dataset
  - Experiments
  - CI/CD
  - Pass@k
  - Pass^k
- **Why it matters**: Prevents regressions when modifying prompts, models, or agent code in production.
## Key Points
### Looks good to me is not a test suite
- **Explanation**: Relying on manual spot-checking of a few agent runs leads to unexpected production failures when users use the agent in novel ways.
- **Evidence**: Shipping agent features based on 3 manual test runs.
- **Practical implication**: Establish automated evaluation suites before shipping AI agents.
### Code evals are fast, free, and brittle
- **Explanation**: Deterministic functions check formatting and exact matches in milliseconds without API costs.
- **Evidence**: String matching and JSON parsing checks.
- **Practical implication**: Use code evals for structure and format; use LLM judges for meaning.
### LLM judges understand meaning but make mistakes
- **Explanation**: Using a second LLM to grade outputs against a rubric handles semantics but can be non-deterministic and costly.
- **Evidence**: LLM judge evaluating grounding and tone.
- **Practical implication**: Validate LLM judges against human-labeled golden datasets.
### Human labels form the golden dataset
- **Explanation**: Humans remain the gold standard for quality judgment.
- **Evidence**: Annotating 16 traces with actionability labels in Phoenix.
- **Practical implication**: Build a golden dataset of 20-100 human-labeled examples to test your judges.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Swiss Cheese Model of Quality
- **How it works**: Stacking multiple imperfect evaluation layers so that errors are caught by at least one layer.
- **Components**:
  - Automated evals
  - Manual transcript review
  - Production monitoring and A/B testing
- **When to use**: When building production-grade AI agents requiring high reliability.
### Five Parts of a Good Eval Prompt
- **How it works**: Structuring an LLM judge prompt for consistent, reliable grading.
- **Components**:
  - The judge's role
  - Explicit criteria
  - Data clearly marked
  - Labeled examples
  - A constrained answer
- **When to use**: When writing custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators.
## Examples & Case Studies
### An agent searching for Tesla data returned a report about an 18th-century inventor instead.
- **Illustrates**: Confidently wrong model behavior.
- **Lesson**: Without evals, model hallucinations and confabulations go unnoticed until customers experience them.
### Adding XML tags around few-shot examples flipped the evaluator's classification results from all negative to correct.
- **Illustrates**: Prompt sensitivity in LLM judges.
- **Lesson**: Treat eval prompts like code; structure data clearly using XML tags to avoid parsing confusion.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Read your traces before writing evals.
  - Write code evals for structure and format.
  - Add LLM-as-a-judge evals for semantic quality.
- **Strategic**:
  - Build a golden dataset with human-labeled examples.
  - Run experiments when changing prompts or models.
  - Integrate test suites into CI/CD pipelines.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How many examples are needed in the golden dataset?
  - How to balance precision and recall in LLM judges?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Tracing takes about five lines of code using OpenInference. (technical)
- Human-human agreement on qualitative tasks (Cohen's kappa) is often low (0.2-0.3). (statistical)
## Notable Quotes
> "Without evals, every change is a gamble." (at 11:49)
> ""Looks good to me" is not a test suite." (at 10:12)
> "A prompt change you haven't measured is a vibe." (at 165:10)
## Compressed Summary
- Traces are logs; evals are tests for AI.
- Combine code evals, LLM judges, and human review.
- Build golden datasets from human annotations.
- Run experiments to validate prompt and model changes.
- Integrate eval test suites into CI/CD pipelines.
- **Keywords**: evals, observability, phoenix, llm-as-a-judge, testing
- **Core insight**: Systematic evaluation using traces, code evals, and LLM judges replaces guesswork and vibes with rigorous testing for AI agents.
